title: What a prophet is
hookLine: one who speaks for God, usually uncomfortably, to their own people

lines: A STORY ABOUT A STOLEN LAMB.
cards: A king has done something terrible. He took another man's wife, and when she became pregnant, he arranged for her husband to die in battle. Nobody at court will say a word.
Then a man named Nathan comes and tells the king a story: a rich man with huge flocks steals a poor man's only lamb, a lamb the poor man's children loved, to serve to a guest. The king is furious.
That man deserves to die, he says. And Nathan looks at King David and says four words, in the King James Bible: "Thou art the man." A new block, and a question: what is a prophet?

teach.b: In everyday speech, a prophet predicts the future; in the Bible, that's a small part. The Greek prophetes means one who speaks for, or speaks forth: a spokesperson.
The Hebrew is navi, and some scholars think it means one who is called, or one who calls out. Either way, the job is less fortune-telling than forth-telling: saying what God sees, now, out loud.
And they spoke mostly to their own people: kings, priests and neighbors, about their own injustice: the poor cheated in the market, widows ignored, worship that was all show. It was rarely welcome.
Jeremiah was beaten and thrown in a pit. Amos was told to go home.
Some weren't professionals at all: Amos said he was no prophet, nor a prophet's son, but a herdsman and a tender of fig trees. And they weren't only stern.
The same voices that warned also comforted: Isaiah, tomorrow's prophet, speaks of swords beaten into plowshares, and of a God who will not forget his people even if a mother could forget her child.

In Christian Bibles, the prophets close the Old Testament: Isaiah, Jeremiah, Ezekiel and Daniel, called the major prophets because their books are long, with Lamentations beside Jeremiah, then twelve shorter ones.
Jewish Bibles arrange them differently, and count books like Joshua and Kings among the prophets too.
In Matthew's Gospel the crowds call Jesus a prophet, and he says, "A prophet is not without honour, save in his own country, and in his own house."
Christians honor him as more than a prophet, and also see him standing in this line.

how: Christians read the prophets throughout the church year, especially in Advent and Lent, and many churches see the prophets' call for justice as part of their own work with the poor; Jewish communities read a passage from the Prophets, the haftarah, every Sabbath.

games.q: what's inside the word — tap the pairs.
p: one who speaks for, or forth
one called, or one who calls
a herdsman, not a prophet's son

s: a biblical prophet is mainly someone who predicts the future
mostly they spoke forth what God saw now: injustice, false worship, and hope.
the prophets mostly spoke to their own people
to their own kings, priests and neighbors, about their own wrongs.
the major prophets are called major because they matter more
major means their books are long; the twelve minor prophets are shorter.

games.q: you're Nathan. the king has covered up a terrible wrong, and everyone at court is silent. what do you do?
o: tell the king a story, then say thou art the man.
complain about him to others in private.
games.why: Nathan tells a story about a stolen lamb, lets the king judge it, and then says "thou art the man." truth to power, to his own king.

practice: Think of something someone told you recently that stung, a criticism from a friend, a hard word from a boss, and notice the defense forming. Set it aside a moment and ask honestly: is there any truth in it, not all of it, just any?
Hold that piece without arguing, and if you pray, ask for ears to hear it.

wordCard.voice: Prophet. Navi in Hebrew, prophetes in Greek: one called to speak for God, usually uncomfortably, and usually to their own people.
